WORLD ART DIRECTION

Painterly, tidal, restrained.

Weathered maritime realism, visible brushwork, slate and sea-glass colour, one warm practical light, fog with real depth.

Illustrated, weathered, graphic.

Dry-brush pigment, charcoal contour, weathered paper, sea-glass blue and one lantern-orange accent.

Can Maren call a tide she has never stood in?
No. CANON-002 is explicit, a caller cannot move a tide she has not stood in, and the song costs hearing with every verse. Maren stood the harbour tide in scene 2 of Saltlight, so the verse rising in scene 4 holds. Open water past the Vigil is outside her reach until she stands in it, and each call she makes costs her another verse of hearing.
CANON-002 · Tide-calling CANON-031 · The night the bells sank Maren · sheet v4

Who collects rent in the Drowned Quarter?
The canon doesn't answer this, and it won't guess.
Searched all 42 entries. CANON-021 comes closest: rent in the Quarter is still collected, "nobody says by whom." No rule, faction, or timeline entry names the collector. Answering now would be invention, and it would ripple into every production that touches the Quarter.

OPEN THREAD · CANON-043

Who collects rent in the Drowned Quarter?

I think it's the Ebb Council, quietly. They'd never admit it.
It can work, but it leans on CANON-013: the Council is publicly prudent, privately terrified of the verse. Collecting drowned rent means touching the water they fear. Two ways to hold both: they collect through intermediaries, or the rent collects itself and the Quarter punishes debt. The first needs a name; the second deepens the dread but answers nothing.
checked: CANON-013 · CANON-021 · CANON-031, no contradiction if the intermediary is named
The bellkeepers. And nobody has ever seen one collect.
Drafted, the bellkeepers collect for the Council under a name nobody writes down. CANON-013 gains a cross-reference; the Quarter keeps its menace. The entry is on the right.

CANON-043 · lore
The bellkeepers' rent
Rent in the Drowned Quarter is collected by the bellkeepers on behalf of the Ebb Council, an arrangement the Council does not acknowledge and no tenant has ever witnessed. Debt in the Quarter is always settled; how is not spoken of.
links: CANON-021 CANON-013 · amended The Drowned Quarter

NEW CANON ENTRY · WILL BE CANON-044

Say what should be true.

ChatForm
Bells raised from the harbour should remember the verse somehow. Salvaged bell-iron feels like it should matter.
It fits. CANON-031 already has the bells ringing unstruck the night the city sank. If bell-iron keeps a memory of the verse, struck salvage would repeat the last thing it heard. That gives the Bell Market's great bell a reason and Bray's salvage a market. One caution: keep it one-way: iron remembers, it doesn't answer. Answering is the Chorister's ground.
checked: CANON-031 · CANON-002 · the Bell Market, no contradiction if memory is passive
Passive, yes. And it fades, a bell forgets in a season.
Drafted with the season limit, which keeps salvage urgent. The entry is on the right.

The Ferryman

Refuses payment in coin, only in secrets. Drafted from your sentence; everything below is proposed, not settled.

Appearanceproposed
A coat of patched sailcloth, pockets sewn shut. Face kept in the lantern's shadow, deliberately, you suspect.
Relationshipsproposed
Knows Bray's biggest secret already. Odile has never once used the ferry. Worth asking why.
Canon rulesproposed
A secret paid is a secret kept. He can cross water the tide won't touch: the one route the Chorister can't hear.
Voice · writtenproposed
Asks questions like tolls. Never repeats what he's told, aloud.

I want a quiet beat between the verse rising and the pier: Maren below deck, deciding whether to answer it.
Three shots, no dialogue: close on her hands stilling the charts; the thread at her collar starting to glow as the song reaches her; she stands, decision made, face out of frame. About 11 seconds, three shots.
canon check: the thread glows only when a tide is callable · CANON-002 holds here. Keeping the Chorister unseen; scene 5 lands harder for it.
Longer on the middle shot, the glow should feel like a question. And she takes the lantern with her.
Done, shot 2 to 5 seconds. The lantern ties her exit to Sereth's gutter in scene 4; I've noted the prop for continuity. Draft updated on the right.

NEW LOCATION

Describe the place. It pushes back.

ChatForm
The bell market, where they sell whatever the divers bring up. It should feel like a church that forgot it was one.
Then keep the bones: stalls in the nave, the auction block where the altar stood, and the great bell still hanging, which rings by itself on spring tides. Bray would sell here; the Ebb Council would tax it.
canon check: bells rang unstruck the night the city sank · CANON-031. A bell that still rings is a scar, not decoration.
Yes. And nobody ever stands under the bell.
Added as a custom, the kind nobody explains in dialogue. The market's crowd just flows around that one empty flagstone. Draft updated.

not started
An overview is one logline and a spine. It steers scene drafting and pass packing, and it never overwrites a scene you have locked.
LOGLINE
One sentence. What happens, to whom, and what it costs.
SPINE
Two or three lines. Enough to tell whether a scene belongs.
OR SKIP IT
Draft a scene first and let the spine catch up. Nothing downstream requires an overview to exist.

The missing night

This one opens well and stops. They reach the street the ledger says is missing, and then the episode has nowhere to leave the audience.

STORY · SEASON 1 · DIRECTION

What this season does differently.

Vertical and at night, so it has to read at arm’s length. Less fog than the world wants.
Then this season narrows the world look rather than replacing it: same palette and brushwork, closer framing, and fog pulled back so faces survive a phone screen. I have written it as three lines against The Undersong’s v3.
✓ read art direction v3 · world look unchanged · nothing written
Keep shaping the direction… ↵ send
Season Episodes Arcs Direction
The Undersong · master lookv3 · inherited
Painterly, tidal, restrained. Slate and sea-glass, one warm practical light, fog with real depth.
This season narrows it3 lines · would change
Framing sits closer. A face fills more of a vertical frame than it would of a wide one.
Fog is pulled back one stop. It reads as depth on a cinema screen and as mud on a phone.
Night is lit by one practical, never ambient blue.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO
It does not change The Undersong’s look, and nothing made for Saltlight or Undertow moves. A season narrows the world it is in; it never edits it.

A coastal city where a drowned god still sings, and some people can hear it.
Then the city has learned to live around the song, bells muffled, harbours rebuilt twice. I've called it The Undersong for now; one word from you changes it. Who hears the song first: someone who profits from it, someone haunted by it, or someone whose job it is?
seeded: title · logline · tone (quiet dread) · all proposed, nothing locked
Whose job it is. A tide-caller, the last one. She's paid to move water, but she hears the verse underneath it.
A working woman, not a chosen one, that keeps the dread quiet. I've sketched her as Maren Kest, and given the harbour a counterweight: the Vigil, a lighthouse whose keeper listens for what shouldn't answer back. Two threads I've left open on the right. Pull either one when you're ready.

STORY OVERVIEW · NARRATIVE GAME

Find the spine, then the forks.

The player is Ilo. One salvage run into the Quarter at record low water, out by dawn. Bray comes along. The song is waking.
That's a clean dramatic question: does Ilo answer the song, or get out. Two chapters would carry it — the run in, the run back. The real choice is whether Ilo tells Bray what the song said.
canon check: CANON-002 says hearing costs a verse. If Ilo hears it in chapter 1, that cost is yours to spend somewhere. I've kept it as a delayed consequence, not a rewrite of the rule.
Yes — and neither ending should be the "right" one. Answering the song can't be a fail state.
Held: both endings stay equally valid, and neither writes back to the world. If a sequel ever needs one to be true, you'll promote it explicitly. The proposal is beside you — chapter 1 has six scenes, one merge, two endings.
